## Time and Tsibbles

1.  Retail_ts contains the U.S Census Bureau's monthly retail trade survey with retail sales seasonally adjusted and non seasonally adjusted from 1992 to 2026. Retail_ts stacks two series using series_id. Can_gas contains monthly natural gas production in Canada measured in billions of cubic meters, from January 1960 to February 2005. canadian_gas holds only the one series in volume and has no key.

    ```{r}
    #/ include : false
    library(tidyverse)
    library(fpp3)
    retail_raw <- read_csv("data/retail_sales_raw.csv")

    head(retail_raw)



    retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>
      select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>
      pivot_longer(cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA), names_to = "series_id", values_to = "sales")

    head(retail_raw_long)

    retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
      mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
      as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)

    library(fpp3)

    retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
      mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
      as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)

    head(retail_ts)
    has_gaps(retail_ts)

    head(canadian_gas)

    key_vars(canadian_gas)
    index_var(canadian_gas)

    can_gas <- canadian_gas |>
      select(Month, Volume)

    has_gaps(can_gas)
    head(can_gas)

    can_gas_recent <- can_gas |>
      filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan"))

    head(can_gas_recent)

    can_gas_recent <- can_gas_recent |>
      mutate(year    = year(Month),
             month   = month(Month, label = TRUE),
             quarter = quarter(Month))
    can_gas_recent |>
      as_tibble() |>
      group_by(month) |>
      summarize(avg_volume = mean(Volume))

    can_gas_recent |>
      mutate(next_month           = Month + 1,
             same_month_last_year = Month - 12) |>
      head()

    can_gas_q <- can_gas |>
      filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>
      index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>
      summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))
    head(can_gas_q)

    can_gas_q |> autoplot(Volume)

    retail_ts |> autoplot(sales)

    retail_ts |>
      autoplot(sales) +
      labs(
        title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
        subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
        x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
      ) +
      theme_minimal()

    can_gas |> autoplot(Volume)


    can_gas |>
      autoplot(Volume) +
      labs(
        title = "Canadian gas producution",
        x = "Months", y = "Volume", color = NULL) +
      theme_minimal()

    can_gas |>
      autoplot(Volume) +
      labs(
        title = "Canadian gas producution",
        x = "Months", y = "Volume", color = NULL) +
      geom_point() + 
      geom_smooth()
    ```

    First a Tsibble was created. Runs cleanly with no gaps. Then a New tsibble can_gas created and runs with no gaps. We then created a tsibble for observations past January 2020, added a year month label, and changed the frequency by dropping an observation. The reason we sum the monthly values for gas production rather than taking the mean is so that we don't skew our data by taking means. Mean numbers can sometimes take our outliers and distort the data. After converting, the quarterly data is no longer seasonal. We then note that the NSA series contains large spikes upwards and downwards with more stable growth in between. This line is very seasonal with the same flow each year. The Sa does not show this same repetition. Both series follow the same upwards trend over the long run and are not impacted by seasonal differences. In the last chart, points and a smooth line were added to look at seasonality a bit better and to see the dip in the 80's-90's more clearly.

\##

Transformations

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |> 
  mutate("log_volume" = log(Volume))

can_gas |>
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian gas producution",
    x = "Months", y = "Log Volume", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_nsa <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  mutate("log_sales" = log(sales))

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Retail sales",
    x = "Months", y = "Sales", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Retail Sales",
    x = "Months", y = "Log sales", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_direct = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume)
  )
can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(
    title = "Growth rate Percentage of Volume for Canadian Gas",
    x = "Months", y = "Growth %", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(growth_gap = abs(growth_direct-growth_logdiff))

can_gas |> 
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(
    title = "Growth ",
    x = "Months", y = "Growth % of gap", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










```

At first we add the log of volume and it doesn't help produce better information about the series. The original series was relatively more linear and I would not conclude that from 1960-2020 the swings goes progressively bigger. We then log retail and see a stronger overall series. The growth rate is much clearer and the flow is more linear. We then look at the seasonally adjusted retail versus the non and we see less month to month large shifts with seasonality adjusted. We then tried taking the log difference approximation and it works out okay although the growth % is positive compared to the direct with negative values. The last thing we did here was look at noise and found that the Seasonally adjusted is nosier due due to the smaller movements in the month to month changes. The NSA contains larger spikes that we know are seasonal disruptions so we can assume for those to not be white noise.

\##

Seasonality

```{r}

retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id =="RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales)


retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id =="RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in Canadian Gas Production",
    y = "Log Volume"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production",
    y = "log(Volume)"
  )

retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()

retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()

sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
    x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))

report(can_gas_fit)


can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24)

```

Here we see the SA shows the seasonally adjusted millions of dollars with less month to month shifts and disregards to the large spike for the most part due to seasonality. We then look at seasonality in canadian gas and see that the volume is lower in the summers. We would assume this to be because natural gas is often used to heat homes and homes don't need as much heat over the summers. Then we jump back to the retail side and see that the seasonal factor is highest in January. In January sales are roughly 15-20% higher than the trend. Along with this, the seasonal swings decrease slightly over time. When we compare the adjustment to the official they are very comparable, except for the seasonal swings appear to get larger as the series goes along. This becomes apparent when the series gets closer to 2020/Covid. We then estimate the monthly growth rate of gas production which is 0.4% with June having the most significant seasonal effects. After this we charted the fitted against the actual for canadian gas. The fitted does a good job overall trending upward, but misses the shape of the actual log volume. The actual follows an exponential growth whereas the gitted is very linear and therefore misses the early low values and the middle flat section of the trend. The last thing we do in this section is look at the residuals and find that the residuals do not look like white noise. We use the Ljung-Box test to conclude that we can reject the null hypothesis of white noise with a p value of less than 0.05.

\##

Forecast Evaluation

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))
table(gas_cv_fc |>
        accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
        group_by(.model) |>
        summarize(across(c(MAE, RMSE), mean)))

errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)

gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)
gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))

```

First we ran an expanding window with our first date in January 1980 and last in March 2005. The results from this were the seasonal naive foretasted with lower errors. The MAE is lower for both models and therefore the two metrics agree. We also ran a rolling window and proceeded with a DM test to test for accuracy. The DM statistic was -31.278 and p value was 2.2e-16. Using this output we can reject the null of equal forecast accuracy between the two models. The final thing we looked at was the MAE and RSME for Snaive and tslm for a rolling window compared to the expanding. We found that with a rolling window our tslm model became more accurate. This is because our results become more linear with a rolling window instead of the exponential results we might see in an expanding.

\##

Reflection

The residuals from part 4.4 c showed that there were large gaps in the trend with large gaps between the actual and residual data. This would lead us to believe that there is more to be modeled that isn't just white noise. We aren't specifying to the full potential of our model. I would expect a model that could capture that missing data to look more like a mean relation with less gaps between residuals and actual data.
